about.title: About
about.name: Alex
about.summary: Create Cutting-Edge Apps with a Focus on Componets, Accessibility, and UX
full: I've gone from a LAMP stack developer to someone who focuses on UX/UI with growing brand awareness. I've worked on codebases ranging from small to large, from legacy to new, and from small state-sized to large global companies.

Alex can identify and resolve issues with persistence and dedication and is an exceptional communicator excited about learning software while collaborating with others. They can be resourceful, reliable, and professional. Alex is known for their strong work ethic and working well in a fast-paced environment. Some of their skills include ES6 JavaScript, React, Next.js and TanStack, S/CSS, and Sitecore.

Before I did this professionally, I explored it as a hobby, working on fan sites for some of my favorite shows. In the mid-2000s, people made them for fun. Websites had personality, even when the design was rough.

In 2010, I decided to finish my degree and go into web development. If you're stuck in life, why not do something you enjoy? That started my career. In 2013, I graduated from Champlain College and started my first job at HMC Advertising a month later.

At HMC, I delved into what it means to work with clients. Learning how data and design can influence people and where dark design patterns can manipulate them was an eye-opener and shaped how I understood marketing practices. The sites I developed though, Snap, Parent Up, My Healthy VT, Good Food Truck, and 802Quits were the opposite of those ideas. They were meant to help people, not manipulate them into buying something. It was great to find out that the data said that they were. More people were visiting the new or updated sites than their previous versions.

In 2016, I joined Dealer.com, one of the largest (at least at the time) tech companies in Vermont, and worked with a team assigned to Suberu of New England. This was the first time I worked in a product company, and when ideas like CI/CD and React was starting to take hold. I realized that componentizing was the direction we should go. Create something that can be customized and used in different places and situations, instead of relying on page based design.

However, in just a year and a half, I would be laid off. This is the longest year I was without work, but I was still learning. I delved into Unity with C# since I had the understood the language from college. I didn't make anything great or something I would sell. Instead, I learned how interactivity can change your perception - lack of a better phrase - of the thing you are interacting with. Something that feels like you can hold can make something not boring.

At the end of this year, I moved to Boston and started work with a UX team at Mapfre. This was the largest corporation I've worked for, and it had its own brand of challenges, but the ideas I had learned before were in use here. I've always liked how we could deconstruct the most basic of elements (both in science and in development). How does the interaction of a basic form mean someone will or will not fill it? How does the same form's layout do the same thing? Here I delved more into accessibility and saw how we could help someone complete what they need to do. But that's not just it; I also found how Design Systems were the future.

I don't know if you remember, but the 2010's design styles were going in a direction that, yes, made things more usable, but the personality was gone. Many sites were using either Bootstrap, MaterialUI, or Foundation. CSS3 gave us so many tools to make great design, but we were falling back to these same design, component libraries and trends. It's still a problem today but design systems allow the brand to be in charge. So, that's how Breakpoint was born. A system that brought together components, brand, voice, and iconography. It was a dream to share it with the non-US-based companies within Mapfre, but that never happened.

Around 2020, I felt it was time to move on and get back to a small company where I felt I had a voice. I joined Thankful, which by now has been gobbled up by Gladly, was and will be the only time I will work with a startup. What did I learn here? Not much, other than not working in a framework because the CTO doesn't understand them is not a good excuse.

Finally, we've reached the present, and I may have found the type of work I should do. Velir is a fully remote digital agency. I have really loved doing different kinds of projects with different kinds of people. It allows you to learn more and not become stagnate on what you can do. Plus, its easier to share things I'm actually glad to work on. Accessibility, React, and the multiple CMS we've worked on have shown us the multitude of clients that need help.

But what am I looking for in the future? I'm not sure. I would love to create more art, more interactions, and even see the weird internet come back. Places like NeoCities bring back the weird and fun, and maybe, I'll create something that brings that back.

• I love art and draw a lot.
  • Indie games is where it's at now. Balatro, Hades, Rimworld and some of the best games out there.
  • Movies have facinated me since I was young. David Lynch's work shaped my love of sureal and the weird
  • Music? oh course. Right now I'm into synth, goth, post-punk, and anything dark and weird.
